The Analysis of the Mode of Conveying Conversion.
Therein, what is the mode of conveying conversion?
It is this: "In one footing."
“Exert yourselves, strive on,
apply yourselves to the Buddha’s teaching;
shake off the army of Death.”
“Like an elephant in a reed-hut” refers to the elephant simile.
“Exert yourselves, strive! is the proximate cause for energy.
“Yoke yourselves to the Buddha’s teaching! is the proximate cause for concentration.
“Shake off the army of Death, as an elephant shakes down a reed-hut”—this is the proximate cause for wisdom (*paññā*).
“Exert yourselves, strive!”—this is the proximate cause for the faculty of energy (*vīriyindriya*).
“Devote yourselves to the Buddha’s teaching!”—this is the proximate cause for the faculty of concentration (*samādhindriya*).
“Shake off the army of Death, as an elephant shakes off a reed-hut”—this is the proximate cause (*padaṭṭhāna*) for the faculty of wisdom (*paññindriya*).
These are the proximate causes; they are the teaching.
They are the application for beings who are applying themselves to yoga, or the undertaking for those who are already engaged in it.
In that regard, those who do not apply themselves do so because of negligence as their root.
That negligence is twofold: rooted in craving and rooted in ignorance.

Therein, that which is rooted in ignorance is the lack of knowledge by which one is shrouded and does not understand the objects of knowledge—that the five aggregates are subject to arising and passing away; this is what is rooted in ignorance.
That which is rooted in craving is threefold: one who seeks the arising of unarisen wealth falls into negligence;
one who guards arisen wealth and one who indulges in it fall into negligence.
Thus, this fourfold negligence in the world is of one kind through ignorance and of three kinds through craving.
In this context, ignorance has the mental body as its proximate cause;
craving has the physical body as its proximate cause.
For what reason? Because there is attachment to the realms of existence that possess form, and delusion regarding those that are formless.
Therein, the material body is the aggregate of form, and the mental body consists of the four immaterial aggregates.
By what kind of clinging (*upādāna*) are these five aggregates possessed of clinging? They are possessed of clinging through craving (*taṇhā*) and ignorance (*avijjā*).
Therein, craving constitutes two kinds of clinging: clinging to sensual pleasures (*kāmupādāna*) and clinging to rules and observances (*sīlabbatupādāna*).
Ignorance consists of two types of clinging: clinging to views and clinging to the doctrine of self.
Those aggregates accompanied by these four types of clinging constitute suffering.
The four types of clinging constitute the origin.
The five aggregates are suffering.
For their full understanding and for their abandonment, the Blessed One teaches the Dhamma for the full understanding of suffering and the abandonment of its origin.
In this regard, there is a threefold negligence rooted in craving which seeks the arising of wealth not yet arisen, and [seeks to increase] that which has already arisen...
He both guards enjoyments for the sake of their use and brings them about for that purpose; through his penetration of these, guarding and withdrawing [from them] constitute serenity (*samatha*).
How does this come about?

When he knows sensual pleasures as gratification from the perspective of gratification, as danger from the perspective of danger, and as escape from the perspective of escape; and when he knows their degradation, their defilement, and their cleansing, as well as the benefit in renunciation.
In this context, that which is inquiry and investigation is insight (*vipassanā*).
These two phenomena—serenity (*samatha*) and insight—reach the fulfillment of their development.

When these two phenomena are being developed, two phenomena are abandoned: craving (*taṇhā*) and ignorance (*avijjā*). When these two phenomena are abandoned, the four types of clinging (*upādāna*) cease.

With the cessation of clinging, there is the cessation of existence; with the cessation of existence, the cessation of birth; with the cessation of birth, aging and death, sorrow, lamentation, pain, grief, and despair cease.
Thus occurs the cessation of this entire mass of suffering.
Thus, the two preceding truths are suffering and its origin, while serenity and insight are the path.
The cessation of existence is nibbāna; these are the four truths.
Therefore the Blessed One said: "Exert yourselves, strive!
"Just as when the root is uninjured and firm..."
Even a tree that has been cut down grows again; even so,
as long as the underlying tendency of craving is not uprooted,
this suffering arises again and again.
This is the underlying tendency to craving.
Of what kind of craving?
Of the craving for existence.
That which is the condition for this phenomenon is ignorance (*avijjā*).
For with ignorance as condition, there is craving for existence (*bhavataṇhā*).
These two are the defilements: craving and ignorance.
Those four types of clinging and the aggregates accompanied by clinging through those four types of clinging—this is suffering.
The four types of clinging are the origin.
The five aggregates are suffering.
The Blessed One teaches them the Dhamma for full understanding and for abandoning—namely, for the full understanding of suffering and the abandoning of its origin.
That by which one eradicates the underlying tendency of craving is serenity (*samatha*);
that by which one wards off ignorance, the condition for the underlying tendency of craving, is insight (*vipassanā*).
These two things reach the fulfillment of their development: serenity and insight.
Therein, the fruit of serenity is the liberation of mind through the fading away of lust; the fruit of insight is the liberation by wisdom through the fading away of ignorance.
Thus, the first two truths—suffering and its origin—are [the objects of] serenity and insight, while the path consists of serenity and insight, and the two liberations are cessation.
These are the four truths.
Therefore the Blessed One said: “Just as at the root...
“The non-doing of all evil, ...”
The undertaking of what is wholesome,
the complete purification of one’s own mind—
this is the teaching of the Buddhas.
"All evil" refers to the three types of misconduct: bodily misconduct, verbal misconduct, and mental misconduct;

these are the ten unwholesome courses of action: killing living beings, taking what is not given, sexual misconduct, false speech, malicious speech, harsh speech, idle chatter, covetousness, ill will, and wrong view. These consist of two kinds of kamma: volition and the mental factors associated with it.
In this regard, whatever constitutes the destruction of life, malicious speech, and harsh speech—this originates from hatred (*dosa*).
Whatever constitutes taking what is not given, sexual misconduct, and false speech—this originates from greed (*lobha*). Whatever constitutes frivolous chatter—this originates from delusion (*moha*).
These seven factors constitute volitional action (*cetanā-kamma*).
Covetousness is greed, the unwholesome root;
ill will is hatred, the unwholesome root;
wrong view is the wrong path.
These three factors constitute mental action (*cetasika-kamma*).
Therefore it was said: "Volitional action (*cetanā-kamma*) is mental action.
When an unwholesome root proceeds to its application, it goes toward one of four wrong courses: through desire, hatred, fear, or delusion.
In this context, that which goes astray through desire is originated by greed;
that which goes astray through hatred is originated by hatred;
and that which goes astray through fear and delusion is originated by delusion.
Therein, greed is abandoned by means of the foul;
hatred, by means of loving-kindness;
and delusion, by means of wisdom.
Likewise, greed is abandoned by equanimity;
hatred by loving-kindness and compassion;
and delusion reaches its abandonment and disappearance through sympathetic joy.
Therefore the Blessed One said: “The non-doing of all evil.
All evil means the eight wrongnesses: wrong view, wrong intention, wrong speech, wrong action, wrong livelihood, wrong effort, wrong mindfulness, and wrong concentration; this is called all evil.
The non-performance, the non-doing, and the non-transgression of these eight wrongnesses—this is called the non-doing of all evil.
When the eight wrong states have been abandoned, the eight right states come into being.
That which is the activity, the performance, and the accomplishment of these eight right states is called "the attainment of the wholesome.
By the phrase "the purification of one's own mind," he shows the activity of developing the past path; when the mind is purified, the five aggregates become purified. For thus the Blessed One said:
“Monks, the holy life is lived under the Tathāgata for the sake of purification of the mind.
For purification is twofold: the abandoning of the hindrances and the uprooting of the underlying tendencies.
There are two planes of purification: the plane of vision and the plane of cultivation. Of these, that which one purifies through penetration is suffering.
That by which one purifies is the origin;
that by means of which one purifies is the path;
that which has been purified is cessation.
These are the Four Truths.
Therefore the Blessed One said: “The non-doing of all evil...
“Indeed, Dhamma protects the one who lives according to Dhamma.”
"Just as a great umbrella [protects] during the rainy season;
such is the benefit of the Dhamma well-practiced:
one who lives by the Dhamma does not go to a state of misery."
"Dhamma" is twofold: restraint of the faculties and the Path.
"Bad destination" is twofold: either the states of deprivation (apāya) are the bad destination in relation to gods and humans, or all forms of rebirth are the bad destination in relation to Nibbāna.
In this context, that which is the unbroken practice of the virtue of restraint—this Dhamma, when well-practiced, protects one from the states of deprivation.
Thus the Blessed One said:
“Monks, there are these two destinations for one who is virtuous: that of the devas and that of human beings.
And so, in the town of Nāḷandā, Asibandhakaputta the headman spoke thus to the Blessed One.

“Bhante, there are brahmins from the western lands who carry water-pots, wear garlands of water-moss, descend into water, and tend the sacred fire; they claim to expiate those who have died and passed away, to purify them, and to lead them down to heaven.

But can the Blessed One, the Arahant, the Perfectly Enlightened One, do likewise—so that the whole world, upon the breakup of the body after death, might be reborn in a happy destination, a heavenly world?
“In that case, headman, I shall question you about this very matter; answer as you see fit.”

"What do you think, headman? Suppose there were a man here who was a killer of living beings, a taker of what is not given, one of wrong conduct in sensual pleasures, a speaker of falsehood, a speaker of divisive speech, a speaker of harsh speech, a speaker of idle chatter, covetous, ill-willed, and held to wrong view;
and a great crowd of people, having gathered and assembled together, were to entreat him, praise him, and circumambulate him with palms joined, saying: ‘This one...’"
‘May this man, with the breakup of the body, after death, be reborn in a good destination,
a heavenly world. What do you think, headman, would that man, because of the entreaties of the great crowd of people, or because of their praise,
or because of their circumambulating him with palms joined, be reborn in a good destination, a heavenly world, with the breakup of the body, after death?”
“No, venerable sir. “Suppose, headman,
a man were to throw a large, heavy stone into a deep pool of water,
and a great crowd of people were to gather together and assemble there, and with palms joined, were to entreat it, praise it, and circumambulate it.
‘Come up, sir, great rock! Float up, sir, great rock! Float onto dry land, sir, great rock!

What do you think, headman? Would that great rock, because of the entreaties of the great crowd of people, or because of their praises, or because of their circumambulating with palms joined, come up, float up, or float onto dry land?”
“No, venerable sir.

“In the same way, headman, even if a great crowd of people were to gather and assemble, and with palms joined, circumambulate and praise a man who has killed living beings... [and] held wrong view, saying:

‘May this man, with the breakup of the body, after death, be reborn in a good destination, in a heavenly world,’ yet he would still, with the breakup of the body, after death, be reborn in a state of misery, in a bad destination, in the nether world, in hell.”
Then, with the breakup of the body, after death, that man would be reborn in a state of deprivation, a bad destination, a lower realm, even in hell.

What do you think, headman? Suppose here there were another man who abstained from taking life, abstained from taking what is not given, abstained from sexual misconduct, abstained from false speech, and abstained from malicious speech... from harsh speech... [and so on].
Suppose there were one who abstained from speech that leads to harm, abstained from idle chatter, was free from covetousness, possessed a mind without ill will, and held right view.
A great multitude of people would gather together and assemble to entreat him, to praise him, and to circumambulate him with palms joined, saying:
"May this person, upon the breakup of the body after death, be reborn in a state of deprivation, a bad destination, a lower realm, or in hell."
“What do you think, headman? Would that man, because of the entreaties of the great crowd of people, or because of their praises,
or because of their circumambulating him with palms joined, be reborn after the breakup of the body, after death, in a state of deprivation, a bad destination, a lower realm, or in hell?”
“No, venerable sir.
“Suppose, headman, a man were to sink a jar of ghee or a jar of oil into a deep pool of water and break it there.
Whatever shards or potsherds there might be would sink downwards.”
"And suppose there were some ghee or oil in it that was rising upward.
A great crowd of people would gather and assemble, and they would entreat it, praise it, and circumambulate it with palms joined, saying: 'Sink down, sir, ghee and oil! Sink down, sir, ghee and oil!

Go downward, sir, ghee and oil! What do you think, headman? Would that ghee or oil sink down, or sink away, or go downward because of the great crowd of people’s entreaty, praise, or circumambulation with palms joined?"
“No, venerable sir.

“In the same way, headman, even though a great crowd of people might gather and assemble to entreat and praise that person who abstains from taking life … [and so on] … and holds right view, with palms joined in reverence— ”
One could not pursue him with the thought, ‘May this person, with the breakup of the body, after death, reappear in a state of deprivation, a bad destination, a lower realm, or in hell. Rather,
with the breakup of the body, after death, that person would reappear in a good destination, a heavenly world.”
Thus the Dhamma, when well-practiced, protects one from the states of misery.
In this regard, that which is the sharpness and intensity of the Path—this Dhamma, when well-practiced, protects one from all rebirths.
Thus spoke the Blessed One.
“Therefore, for one whose mind is guarded,
whose range is right intention,
and who prioritizes right view— ”
Having understood arising and passing away,
the bhikkhu who has overcome sloth and torpor abandons all states of woe.

In this context, craving and ignorance are the causes of the miserable destinies; those are the four types of clinging. The aggregates accompanied by these four types of clinging constitute suffering (*dukkha*).
The four types of clinging are the origin (*samudaya*).
The five aggregates are suffering; for the full understanding of that suffering and for the abandoning of its origin, the Blessed One teaches the Dhamma.
In this context, the five physical faculties are the proximate cause for craving;
the mind-faculty is the proximate cause for ignorance.
Guarding the five physical faculties, one develops concentration and suppresses craving.
Guarding the mind-faculty, one develops insight and suppresses ignorance.
Through the suppression of craving, two types of clinging are abandoned: clinging to sensual pleasures and clinging to rules and observances.
Through the suppression of ignorance, two types of clinging are abandoned: clinging to views and clinging to the doctrine of self.
When the four types of clinging have been abandoned, two qualities reach full development: serenity and insight.
This is called the holy life (*brahmacariya*).

In this context, the fruit of the holy life consists of the four fruits of asceticism: the fruit of stream-entry, the fruit of once-returning, the fruit of non-returning, and Arahantship, which is the supreme fruit.
These are the four fruits of the holy life (*brahmacariya*).
Thus, the two former truths— suffering and its origin—

and serenity (*samatha*), insight (*vipassanā*), and the holy life as the path, together with the fruits of the holy life and the unconditioned element (*asaṅkhata-dhātu*) which has those as its object, constitute cessation (*nirodha*).
These are the four truths.
Therefore the Blessed One said: “The Dhamma indeed protects.
In that context, that which is protected through penetration is this: suffering.
That from which one protects is the origin;
that by which one protects is the path;
that which one protects is cessation.
These are the four truths.
Therefore the Venerable Mahākaccāyana said: "In a single footing.
The Mode of Conveying the Conversion is concluded.
